claims.claim: Steering the Craft was first published by Eighth Mountain in 1998 and the revised edition was published by Mariner in 2015.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation website, Steering the Craft book page
claims.quote: first published by Eighth Mountain in 1998

claims.claim: 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' was a speech given at the Second Annual Science Fiction Writers' Workshop in 1972 and first published by Pendragon Press in 1973 in a limited run of 776 copies.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation website, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie book page
claims.quote: in 1973 published it in a limited run of 776 copies

claims.claim: Le Guin states as a principle of narrative description that listing is not describing and that only the relevant belongs.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: Listing is not describing. Only the relevant belongs.

claims.claim: Le Guin says what a writer leaves out is infinitely more than what is left in.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in

claims.claim: Le Guin says there has to be white space around the word and silence around the voice.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: white space around the word, silence around the voice

claims.claim: Le Guin glosses crowding as never using ten vague words where two exact words will do.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: never to use ten vague words where two exact words will do

claims.claim: Le Guin warns that overcrowded descriptions clog the story and suffocate themselves.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: Overcrowded descriptions clog the story and suffocate themselves.

claims.claim: Praising Patrick O'Brian's sea battles, Le Guin says everything the reader needs to know is included but nothing more.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: Everything the reader needs to know is included, but nothing more.

claims.claim: Le Guin praises O'Brian's sensory details as intense, brief and precise.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: The sensory details are intense, brief, precise.

claims.claim: Le Guin says there is no optimum sentence length and that the optimum is variety.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: There is no optimum sentence length. The optimum is variety.

claims.claim: Le Guin attributes to teachers, style textbooks, journalists and thriller writers the notion that the only good sentence is a short sentence, and disagrees with it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: the only good sentence is a short sentence

claims.claim: Le Guin calls it a myth that short-sentence prose is more like the way we speak.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: It’s a myth that short-sentence prose is

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in a narrative the chief duty of a sentence is to lead to the next sentence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: the chief duty of a sentence is to lead to the next

claims.claim: Le Guin says a sentence is not working as a narrative sentence if its similes or metaphors are so dazzling that they stop the reader.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: the proper beauty and power of prose

claims.claim: Le Guin says adjectives and adverbs are rich and good and nourishing, and cause obesity in prose only when used lazily or overused.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: ADJECTIVES AND ADVERBS ARE RICH AND good and nourishing.
